title: Prescribed-point high-degree systems with smooth hypersurfaces
statement:
Let $k$ be an algebraically closed field, $X$ a smooth connected affine $k$-scheme of finite type and pure dimension $d\ge2$, and $S\subset X(k)$ a nonempty finite set, also denoting its reduced closed subscheme by $S$. Fix a closed embedding $X\hookrightarrow\mathbf A^N_k$, its projective closure $\overline X\subseteq\mathbf P^N_k$, and $L_n=\mathcal O_{\overline X}(n)$. For all sufficiently large integers $n$, the finite-dimensional vector space
$$V_n=\ker\bigl(\Gamma(\overline X,L_n)\longrightarrow\Gamma(S,L_n|_S)\bigr)$$
has the following properties. Its restrictions generate $L_n$ on $X\setminus S$, and their associated morphism $X\setminus S\to\mathbf P(V_n)$ is an immersion. Writing $\mathfrak m_s$ for the maximal ideal of $\mathcal O_{X,s}$, the map taking the first-order part of a section vanishing on $S$,
$$V_n\longrightarrow\bigoplus_{s\in S}(\mathfrak m_s/\mathfrak m_s^2)\otimes_k(L_n\otimes\kappa(s)),$$
is surjective. There is a nonempty Zariski open $U_{\rm sm}\subseteq\mathbf A(V_n)$ such that, for every $v\in U_{\rm sm}(k)$, the zero scheme $H_v=Z(v|_X)$ is a smooth affine closed subscheme of $X$ of pure dimension $d-1$ containing $S$, and the first-order part of $v$ is nonzero at every $s\in S$. Here $\mathbf A(V_n)$ is affine space with $k$-points $V_n$ (coordinates in any basis). Scheme and morphism notions are those of [def-weil-pbc-scheme-conventions] and [def-weil-scheme-morphism-properties]; invertible sheaves, generation, associated projective morphisms, zero schemes, base change and connectedness are as in [def-sc-invertible-module], [def-weil-pbc-generating-sections], [def-weil-pbc-morphism-to-projective-space-by-sections], [def-pc-zero-scheme], [def-pc-base-change] and [def-weil-connected-scheme]; pure dimension is as in [def-weil-pure-dimension].

source.place: Proof paragraph 2, from projective closure through jet surjectivity and smoothness everywhere

proof.text: Put $Y=\overline X$ and $L=\mathcal O_Y(1)$. The given closed immersion into projective space makes $Y$ projective, hence proper over $k$, and makes $L$ invertible and ample in the absolute sense, with the nonvanishing loci $Y_{s_k}$ of the coordinate sections $s_k\in\Gamma(Y,L)$ forming an affine open cover of $Y$. Since $Y$ is proper over $k$, the affine-loci criterion (with $n=1$ and these sections) makes $L$ ample also in the very-ample-power sense used by the sections-vanishing theorem of step 2. Properness includes finite type; since $k$ is Noetherian, $Y$ is Noetherian. The same finite-type-over-Noetherian theorem applies to the given finite-type $k$-scheme $X$, so $X$ is Noetherian as well. An invertible sheaf and each of its tensor powers are coherent: locally they are free of rank one. Proper coherent cohomology therefore makes $\Gamma(Y,L^{\otimes n})$ finite-dimensional for every $n\ge0$, and its subspace $V_n$ is finite-dimensional.

Apply the sections-vanishing theorem to $(Y,L,S)$. There is $a$ such that for every $n\ge a$, $V_n$ generates $L^{\otimes n}$ on $Y\setminus S$ and gives an immersion there. Restricting the sections and the morphism to the open subscheme $X\setminus S$ preserves generation, and the morphism remains an immersion by composition with the open immersion $X\setminus S\hookrightarrow Y\setminus S$. This proves the first two requested clauses.

Let $\mathcal I$ be the ideal sheaf of $S$ in $Y$. It is quasi-coherent, and so is its square $\mathcal I^2$, computed by squaring the ideal on each affine chart. Both are coherent, since they are quasi-coherent submodules of the coherent module $\mathcal O_Y$ on the Noetherian scheme $Y$. The quotient $\mathcal I/\mathcal I^2$ is coherent as well. For every $n$, tensoring the inclusion and quotient sequence with $L^{\otimes n}$ gives the short exact sequence $0\to\mathcal I^2\otimes L^{\otimes n}\to\mathcal I\otimes L^{\otimes n}\to(\mathcal I/\mathcal I^2)\otimes L^{\otimes n}\to0$: in a frame of the invertible sheaf it is the original exact sequence. The ideal-tensor-sections theorem identifies $\Gamma(Y,\mathcal I\otimes L^{\otimes n})$ with exactly $V_n$, with its given inclusion into $\Gamma(Y,L^{\otimes n})$.

source.place: Tag 01Y1, lemma-coherent-Noetherian-quasi-coherent-sub-quotient; varieties.tex Tag 0FD5, first proof paragraph; schemes.tex Tag 01IN

proof.text: The sheaf $Q_n=(\mathcal I/\mathcal I^2)\otimes L^{\otimes n}$ is supported on the finite set $S$ and is annihilated by $\mathcal I$. Its stalk at $s$ is $(\mathfrak m_s/\mathfrak m_s^2)\otimes_k L_n(s)$, since $X$ is open in $Y$ and $\kappa(s)=k$. Consequently $\Gamma(Y,Q_n)$ is the direct sum of these stalks. Explicitly, take a representative of a germ near $s$ on an open excluding the other points of $S$; it glues with zero on $Y\setminus\{s\}$, because the overlap has zero sheaf. These extensions are unique and their sum gives the asserted inverse to the stalk map. Under this identification the quotient map from the preceding exact sequence sends a section vanishing on $S$ to its first-order parts. Thus the map in the statement is exactly the map on global sections induced by that sequence.

source.place: Paragraph 2, displayed jet map; explicit local ideal and finite-support calculation

proof.text: Apply coherent Serre vanishing on the proper scheme $Y$ with ample $L$ to the fixed coherent sheaf $\mathcal I^2$. For all $n\ge b$ it gives $H^1(Y,\mathcal I^2\otimes L^{\otimes n})=0$. The long exact sequence for the short exact sequence of step 3 then contains $\Gamma(Y,\mathcal I\otimes L^{\otimes n})\to\Gamma(Y,Q_n)\to H^1(Y,\mathcal I^2\otimes L^{\otimes n})=0$. By exactness the first arrow is surjective. Step 4 identifies it with the required simultaneous first-order map from $V_n$. This is the source's infinitesimal-neighbourhood argument, using the ideal $\mathcal I^2$ of the union of the first neighbourhoods.

source.place: Tag 0B5T, lemma-coherent-proper-ample (4); Tag 02O1, lemma-kill-by-twisting; cohomology.tex definition of derived module cohomology

proof.text: Fix $n\ge\max(a,b,0)$. Smoothness gives regular local rings on $X$, so connectedness and nonemptiness (which follows from $S\ne\varnothing$) make $X$ integral. At a closed point $s\in S$, smoothness identifies the dimension of the differential fibre with the topological dimension at $s$; that dimension is $d$, because every nonempty open of the integral finite-type scheme $X$ has dimension $d$. The closed-point cotangent-dimension comparison then gives $\dim_k(\mathfrak m_s/\mathfrak m_s^2)=d>0$. Each summand of the first-order target is therefore nonzero, since $L_n(s)$ is a one-dimensional $k$-vector space.

source.place: Tags 00TT, lemma-characterize-smooth-over-field; 00TR, lemma-rank-omega; properties.tex Tags 0569 and 033N; varieties.tex Tag 0A21 (3)

proof.text: For $s\in S$ let $j_s:V_n\to(\mathfrak m_s/\mathfrak m_s^2)\otimes_k L_n(s)$ be its first-order evaluation. Its zero fibre is a linear closed subspace of $\mathbf A(V_n)$ (in bases, it is defined by the linear coordinate equations of $j_s$). Hence $W=\bigcap_{s\in S}(\mathbf A(V_n)\setminus\ker j_s)$ is open. Choose a nonzero vector in every nonzero summand of the target. Surjectivity in step 5 lifts the resulting tuple to a vector of $V_n$ lying in $W(k)$. Thus $W$ is nonempty, and its $k$-points have nonzero first-order part at every prescribed point.

source.place: Paragraph 2, nonzero first derivative at each s is a nonempty open condition

proof.text: Apply Bertini smoothness to the smooth $k$-scheme $X\setminus S$, the restriction of $L_n$, and the linear restriction map $V_n\to\Gamma(X\setminus S,L_n)$. The vector space is finite-dimensional by step 1; its image generates and its associated map is an immersion by step 2. It yields a nonempty Zariski open $O\subseteq\mathbf A(V_n)$ on which the zero schemes restricted to $X\setminus S$ are smooth. Notice that injectivity of this linear restriction map is not a hypothesis of the cited Bertini theorem.

The coordinate ring of $\mathbf A(V_n)$ is a polynomial ring over $k$, hence a domain. Its nilradical is zero and prime, so its spectrum is irreducible. Every nonempty open in an irreducible space is dense: otherwise it and the complement of its closure would be disjoint nonempty opens, whose complements would be two proper closed subsets covering the space. Thus the two nonempty opens $O$ and $W$ are dense, and $U_{\rm sm}=O\cap W$ is a nonempty open by finite intersection of dense opens.

source.place: Paragraph 2, combining the Bertini and derivative open conditions; elementary parameter-space argument with the cited general algebraic/topological tools

proof.text: Let $v\in U_{\rm sm}(k)$. It vanishes on $S$. Its zero scheme is smooth off $S$ by step 8. At $s\in S$, in a local frame write $v=f$ with $f\in\mathfrak m_s$. The map $\mathfrak m_s/\mathfrak m_s^2\to\Omega^1_{X/k}(s)$ sends $f$ to $df(s)$ and is an isomorphism: its inverse sends $da$ to $a-a(s)$ modulo $\mathfrak m_s^2$; the identity $ab-a(s)b(s)\equiv a(s)(b-b(s))+b(s)(a-a(s))$ verifies the derivation rule. Thus the nonzero first-order part provided by $v\in W(k)$ gives $df(s)\ne0$. The nonzero-relative-differential criterion makes $H_v$ smooth in a neighbourhood of $s$. These neighbourhoods and $H_v\setminus S$ cover $H_v$, proving smoothness everywhere.

source.place: Tag 00TR, lemma-rank-omega, proof; Tag 00T7, lemma-standard-smooth; morphisms.tex Tag 01V7, lemma-smooth-locally-standard-smooth

proof.text: The zero-scheme properties make $H_v$ a locally principal closed subscheme of $X$, containing $S$ scheme-theoretically because $v$ restricts to zero on $S$. A closed immersion is affine, so $H_v$ is affine since $X$ is affine. The nonzero first-order part at any $s\in S$ shows that $v$ is a nonzero section on the integral scheme $X$. Its value at the generic point is nonzero: in each nonempty trivializing affine open the coordinate ring is a domain and embeds in its fraction field, so a section zero generically would be zero on every such open. Thus every local defining function is a nonzero element of a domain, hence a nonzerodivisor. The zero scheme is a nonempty effective Cartier divisor on $X$.

source.place: Tag 0FD6, lemma-bertini, proof paragraph on effective Cartier divisors; morphisms.tex Tag 01SE, lemma-closed-immersion-affine

proof.text: To check purity, fix any irreducible component $D$ of $H_v$, with its reduced induced scheme structure. There are only finitely many components, because $H_v$ is closed in the Noetherian scheme $X$. Remove all the other components from $X$ and call the remaining open $A$. The intersection $D\cap A$ is nonempty: otherwise the irreducible component $D$ would lie in one of the finitely many other components. The divisor $E=H_v\cap A$ and $D\cap A$ therefore have the same underlying topological space; no equality of their scheme structures is needed. By the open-dimension theorem, $A$ is integral of dimension $d$. It is finite type over $k$: since $X$ is Noetherian, $A$ is quasi-compact, hence covered by finitely many distinguished affine opens from finite-type affine charts of $X$, whose coordinate rings are finitely generated over $k$. The local nonzerodivisor equations of step 11 restrict to $A$, so $E$ is a nonempty effective Cartier divisor on $A$. The Cartier dimension-drop theorem gives $\dim E=d-1$, hence $\dim(D\cap A)=d-1$. Finally $D$ is integral and locally of finite type over $k$ (its affine charts are reduced prime quotients of finite-type affine charts of $H_v$). Applying the open-dimension theorem to its nonempty open $D\cap A$ gives $\dim D=d-1$. This holds for every component. The bounds $a$ and $b$ are uniform in $n$, so all conclusions hold for every sufficiently large $n$.

Verified the simultaneous jet map by the ideal-square sequence and finite-support gluing. Against the current unsplit DAG, made Noetherianity of both X and its projective closure explicit and proved purity componentwise using only topological equality with an isolated Cartier divisor, removing the unnecessary reduced-scheme identification and regular-local-domain dependency. Re-read every current cited statement and preserved the item statement and recorded searches.
